title: Space: Eight Minutes to Daylight
description: A star that holds a million Earths, bootprints that never fade, and one small step—Go Deep into space.

questions.question: It lights your day, holds about 1.3 million Earths, and its light takes eight minutes to reach you. What is the closest star to Earth?
questions.explanation: Proxima Centauri is the next-closest star—about 4 light-years away. The Sun is right in our neighborhood, and without it, Earth would be a frozen rock.

questions.question: The Sun lights up our days. What lights up our nights, even though it makes no light of its own?
questions.hint: It looks like a different shape on different nights
questions.explanation: Moonlight is really sunlight bouncing off Moon dust. And the Moon drifts about 1.5 inches farther from Earth every year—about as fast as your fingernails grow!

questions.question: People first walked on the Moon in what year—when about 600 million people watched on TV?
questions.explanation: On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 landed. Around one out of every five people on Earth watched—more than any TV event before it.

questions.question: Who was the first person to step onto the Moon in 1969—and say the words about a small step and a giant leap?
questions.hint: He was the commander of Apollo 11
questions.explanation: Buzz Aldrin followed him 19 minutes later. Armstrong said he meant "a man," not "man"—listen closely to the recording and fans still argue about the missing "a."

questions.question: Neil Armstrong's bootprints are still on the Moon, more than 50 years later! Why haven't rain and weather wiped them away?
choices: Moon dust is sticky like glue
questions.hint: Think about what blows sand around at the beach
questions.explanation: With almost no air, the Moon has no wind or rain. Scientists think the prints could last millions of years, until tiny specks of space dust slowly sand them away.

easterEgg.title: Still there
easterEgg.text: Armstrong's and Aldrin's bootprints, the flag, and even the discarded backpacks are still on the Moon. With almost no air, there is no wind or rain to erase them for millions of years.
